opening.headline: If you want to turn the statement that things seem to have improved after the introduction of AI into numbers, you need to know which indicators should be compared to which baseline.
body: Three months have passed since AI was introduced. Management asks how much better it has become. Team members say things seem to be improving, but there's no record of how long things took before implementation. It is difficult to judge whether to continue or expand the budget based solely on how you feel.

In this lesson, we first summarize four metrics: time, quality, cost, and utilization. Next, we look at why a baseline is needed before introduction, and what is missed when only measuring time savings in the case of document summary introduction.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the types of introduction effect measurement indicators (time, quality, cost)
You can distinguish indicators to compare before and after introduction.

screens.title: All it says is that it seems to be getting better, but there are no numbers.
screens.lead: Read the meeting scene three months after introduction and think about what is lacking.

visual.alt: A meeting scene where team members only talk about their feelings without numbers in front of questions from management.
labels: So how much better has it gotten?

paragraphs: It's been three months since the team adopted AI tools. the management asks. So how much has it improved? Team members responded that they definitely felt more comfortable and improved.

However, there is no record of how long the same took before its introduction. They say things have improved, but there are no numbers to show what the improvements are compared to. It is difficult to judge whether to continue or expand the budget based solely on how you feel.
This class covers what indicators to set and how to explain performance in numbers.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What should have been done before introduction in order to turn the word “improved” into numbers?

screens.outro: Let me first recall my experience.

screens.title: Have you ever tried to explain the results of work improvement in numbers?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: How many hours did it take before and how many hours does it take now?
items.answer: You have to be able to say both before and after in numbers to be able to compare. If you only look at the numbers after, you can't tell the extent of improvement. The number before is the baseline.

items.prompt: Where did you get that number from?
items.answer: To be reliable, measurements must be made using the same method rather than from memory or guesswork. If the measurement method is different before and after, it is impossible to know whether the reason why the numbers look different is because of the tool or the measurement.

items.prompt: How do I know the quality of my results?
items.answer: Time alone won't tell you if the results will be good. Quality indicators such as number of revisions, error rate, and reviewer ratings should be present. It's faster, but if the number of incorrect results increases, it's not an improvement.

screens.outro: To organize the types of numbers, let's start by looking at four types of indicators.

screens.title: Four types of metrics: time, quality, cost, and utilization.
screens.lead: The following flashcards describe four indicators to measure the effectiveness of your adoption: When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

visual.alt: A clock, check, coin, and person icons are placed on the front of four cards.

cards.back: This is an indicator of how much the processing time for the same task has been reduced. Measure it in the same units as the average time per task. It's the first indicator you'll notice, but it alone doesn't tell you if your results are good.

Indicators such as the number of revisions to the results, error rates, and reviewer ratings are indicators of whether the results are improving or at least being maintained. Even if the time has been reduced, if the quality has decreased, it is difficult to see it as an achievement.

We look at the value of subscription or usage costs as well as reduced labor hours. It is easier to compare with before introduction if you look at the unit cost divided by the number of users or processing cases rather than the total amount. We also take into account that the cost increase structure varies depending on the billing method.

This is the percentage of people who actually use it among those who allow it, and how often they use it. If your usage rate is low, you should first determine whether it is a tool or training problem. If the number of users is small, the first three indicators do not represent the overall effect.

The four indicators complement each other. If only time improves and quality deteriorates, it is difficult to see it as an achievement. You can determine whether to expand by looking at cost indicators and utilization together.

screens.outro: Now that we know the indicators, let’s look at the pre-introduction baseline as a basis for comparison.

screens.title: Baseline before introduction: without it, there is no effect.
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the same introduction can be achieved with and without a baseline.

visual.alt: Bar plot comparing interpretability of numbers after introduction with and without baseline.

states.label: no baseline
states.body: The only numbers are that the average work time after introduction is 15 minutes. There is nothing to compare whether these numbers are good or bad. Relying on memory of how long it took before introduction varies from person to person, and cannot answer the objection that it may have been faster without using the tool. So without a baseline, we can't say anything about the effect.

states.label: Has baseline
states.body: The baseline is the current level measured in the same way before introduction. If the average before introduction was 40 minutes and after introduction it was 15 minutes, we can tell the extent of the decrease. In order for the comparison to be fair, the before and after must be done with the same work, same unit, and same conditions. If you do not already have records before introduction, you can create a representative value by manually measuring a small number of tasks. Even if the sample is small, having a baseline is better than not having one, but the limitations of the small sample are also mentioned.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the need for a baseline, let's look at a table of indicators to show why time measurement and quality assessment are needed together.

screens.title: Why work time measurement and quality assessment are needed together
screens.lead: Select the underlined passages in the example indicator table below to see interpretations. Check one by one what judgment each verse leads to.

data.text: Example metric table: The time to create one document is Reduced from 40 minutes before introduction to 15 minutes after introduction. The number of reviewer revisions increased from an average of 2 before introduction to an average of 5 after introduction.. The number of errors pointed out also increased from 3 per month to 9 per month.. The monthly user ratio is 30 percent of team members allowed. The monthly cost is calculated as the sum of subscription fees and usage fees, totaling Unit cost divided by number of cases processed.

marks.span: Reduced from 40 minutes before introduction to 15 minutes after introduction
marks.note: This is a time saving indicator. Since we compared before and after in the same units, we can interpret it. However, this number alone cannot be considered an achievement.

marks.span: The number of reviewer revisions increased from an average of 2 before introduction to an average of 5 after introduction.
marks.note: If time has decreased but revisions have increased, writing time may have been shifted to the review stage. This is why you need to look at time and quality indicators together.

marks.span: The number of errors pointed out also increased from 3 per month to 9 per month.
marks.note: This is a sign that the quality of the results has deteriorated. If errors increase even as time decreases, it is difficult to see real improvement.
This is a utilization indicator. If your usage rate is low, you need to determine whether it's a tool or training issue, and the preceding numbers may be a result of a small number of users.

marks.span: Unit cost divided by number of cases processed
marks.note: If the cost is viewed as a unit cost rather than a total, it is easy to compare it to the labor time cost before introduction.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read your indicators, let's apply them to an example.

screens.title: Commentary: What you miss if you only measure time savings after introducing document summarization
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the limitations of only looking at time savings in the case of introducing document summaries. The numbers below are assumptions for illustration purposes only. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Check case
steps.body: The team introduced a way to read long reports by condensing them using AI. I would like to know the effect of introduction, but let's say we decided to only measure time from the beginning.

steps.title: Baseline before introduction
steps.body: Assume that before introduction, it took an average of 40 minutes to read and summarize a report. This number is a baseline measured in the same way before introduction. There is a baseline so subsequent comparisons can be made.

steps.title: Time since introduction
steps.body: We assume that after introduction this will be reduced to an average of 15 minutes. It has been reduced by 25 minutes, or 62.5%, leaving 37.5% of the time before introduction.

steps.title: Just look at the time indicator
steps.body: Just looking at the time metrics, it looks like a huge improvement. These are good numbers to report to management. But we need to see what these numbers don't tell us.

steps.title: What doesn't appear in the numbers
steps.body: The time indicator does not indicate whether the summary omits key points from the original text or mistranslates figures. If you work based on the wrong summary, the reduced time may come back as more time later.

steps.title: Transfer of Review Burden
steps.body: If the person writing the summary is spending time double-checking the results, the writing time has been reduced, but that time has been moved to the review stage. This movement is not visible if the time indicator only measures the steps in creating the summary. You need to measure the entire job from start to finish to know the actual savings. Include time to read the summary and, if necessary, to go back to the original text.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: In this example, the 25 minutes of time saved is a starting point, not a conclusion. Quality, review time, cost, and utilization must be added to determine success. On the next screen, complete the measurement plan by filling in the missing indicators one by one.

screens.outro: Let's see how to fill in the missing indicators.

screens.title: Commentary: Fill in the missing indicators
screens.lead: The instructor completes the measurement plan by adding quality, cost, and utilization to the time metrics. Select the right arrow to see the steps.

steps.title: Add quality indicators
steps.body: Set up a sample review to check the summary against the original text, counting key omissions and numerical errors. We can't review all of the summaries, so we select a random percentage to check.

steps.title: quality baseline
steps.body: The missing rate in the case of manual summarization is used as a baseline for comparison. The goal is to see whether AI summaries are as accurate as human summaries. It must be reset before introduction in the same way as the time indicator.

steps.title: Add cost indicator
steps.body: Calculate the unit cost by dividing the subscription or usage cost by the number of summaries. Compare this to pre-introduction labor time costs. Let's see how much the time saved is worth in cost. When reading the unit cost, the fact that the number of people increases the cost if it is a subscription type, or the number of requests if it is a token charging system, is also taken into consideration when reading the unit cost.

steps.title: Add utilization indicator
steps.body: See what percentage of your allowed team members actually spend each week. If the usage rate is low, only the results of some team members are reflected, and problems with tools or training must be solved first.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: What you miss when you only look at time savings is poor quality, shifting review burden, lower utilization, and cost-effectiveness. You must first start measuring the four indicators in the same way before introducing them for the numbers to have meaning after introduction.

steps.title: Reporting method
steps.body: Instead of just talking about time savings to management, we report on four metrics in one table. For example, time per summary, number of omissions and errors in sample reviews, unit cost per summary, and percentage of team members writing each week are juxtaposed before and after implementation. Also write down which numbers are assumptions and which numbers are actual measurements.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the measurement plan, let's review the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Without a baseline, there is no effect.
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Read the first question, remembering what it takes to turn the words “improved” into numbers.

paragraphs: In order to turn the word “improved” into numbers, there must be a baseline before introduction. The baseline is the current level measured under the same tasks, same units, and under the same conditions before introduction, and without it, there is no basis to compare whether the numbers after introduction are good or bad. If there are no records before introduction, measure a small number of tasks yourself to create a representative value and write down the limitations.

View time, quality, cost, and utilization together. We need to see not just whether time has been reduced, but whether the quality of results has been maintained, and utilization rates ensure that the effect is representative of the total. And the measurements should start in the same way before introduction. If you start measuring after introduction, comparisons are difficult. Therefore, when deciding on introduction, a measurement plan is also drawn up.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: Measurement begins before introduction. Don't just look at time; look at quality, cost, and utilization as well.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the best response for a team that did not log work hours prior to adoption when trying to measure effectiveness?
options: If the numbers look good after introduction, use that as a baseline.
Since there is no baseline, we give up measuring effectiveness.
Measure a small number of tasks directly to create a representative value and write down the limitations.
Only the satisfaction felt by team members is recorded.
checks.explain: Even with small samples, having a baseline is better than none. Write down the inventory limits together for the same work, same unit, and same conditions.

wrong.0: After introduction, if you use numbers as a standard, there will be no point of comparison.
wrong.1: There is no need to give up because you can compare with representative values you measured yourself.
wrong.3: It is difficult to judge whether to stick to the budget based on how you feel.

checks.intro: Summarize what you just learned by pairing indicators and measurement examples. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the following indicators with their measurement examples.
right: Percentage of allowed team members actually spend each week
Unit cost divided by number of summary cases
Number of key omissions and numerical errors
checks.explain: The four indicators complement each other. If only time is reduced but quality or usage rate is poor, it is difficult to see it as an achievement.

glossary.def: This is an indicator of how much the processing time for the same task has been reduced.
These are indicators of the quality of results, such as number of revisions, error rate, and reviewer evaluation.
It is an indicator that views the value of subscription or usage costs and reduced labor hours as a unit cost.
This is the percentage and frequency of actual use among those who allow it.
This is the current level measured using the same method before introduction and serves as a standard for comparison.

misconceptions.myth: If the time is reduced, it is a success.
misconceptions.fact: Even if time is shortened, it is difficult to call it a success if the quality has decreased or the review burden has increased. We need to see together whether the quality of the results is maintained.

misconceptions.myth: After introduction, you can start measuring.
misconceptions.fact: A pre-introduction baseline is needed for comparison. If there are no records before introduction, you must manually measure a small number of tasks to create at least a representative value.

misconceptions.myth: If the usage rate is high, the performance is high.
misconceptions.fact: Even if you use a lot, the results may not improve. Utilization is meaningful when viewed in conjunction with time, quality, and cost metrics.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Without a baseline, there is no effect.
View time, quality, cost, and utilization together.
Ensure that the quality of results is maintained while saving time.
Measurements start in the same way as before introduction.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What numbers can I use as a baseline for my business before adoption?
